source_text:
Quid? si non solum incerta, sed etiam falsa esse. quae dicit. deo et domino nostro mihi opitulante monstrauero. quid infelicius ista superstitione inueniri potest., quae non modo non exhibet scientiam, quam promittit, atque ueritatem, sed ea dicit, quae uehementer sunt scientiae ueritatique contraria? quod in sequentibus manifestius adparebit. ita enim dicit: iuxta unam uero partem ac latus inlustris illius ae sanctae terrae erat tenebrarum terra profunda et inmensa magnitudine. in qua habitabant ignea corpora. genera scilicet pestifera. hic infinitae tenebrae ex eadem manantes natura inaestimabiles cum propriis fetibus; ultra quas erant aquae caenosae ac turbidae cum suis inhabitatoribus; quarum interius uenti horribiles ac uehementes cum suo principe et genitoribus. rursum regio ignea et corruptibilis cum suis ducibus et nationibus. pari more introrsum gens caliginis ac fumi plena, in qua morabatur inmanis princeps omnium et dux habens circaseinnumerabiles principes, quorum omnium ipse erat mens atque origo: haeque fuerunt naturae quinque terrae p\'estiferae.
. Si aerium uel etiam aetherium corpus diceret esse naturam dei, profecto inrideretur ab omnibus. qui sapientiae ueritatisque naturam per nulla spatia locorum distentam atque diffusam sine ulla mole magnam et magnificam nec in parte minorem et in parte maiorem, sed per omnia aequalem summo patri. nec aliud habentem hic et aliud alibi, sed ubique integram. ubique praesentem qualicumque acie iam serenioris mentis intueri ualent.
thought_title: Mani's five pestilential natures and the folly of a bodily God
orientation: Augustine has just shown that Mani demands belief in unproved claims; now he quotes Mani's description of the land of darkness and its five natures, then argues that any bodily account of God's nature is absurd.
pass_a_gloss: What? If I shall have shown, with God and our Lord helping me, that the things which he says are not only uncertain but also false, what can be found more unhappy than this superstition, which not only does not exhibit the knowledge which it promises and the truth, but says those things which are violently contrary to knowledge and truth? This will appear more clearly in the things that follow. For he speaks thus: Along one part indeed and side of that illustrious and holy land there was a land of darkness, deep and of immense magnitude, in which dwelt fiery bodies, pestilential kinds of course. Here infinite darknesses flowing from the same nature, immeasurable, with their own offspring; beyond which were muddy and turbid waters with their own inhabitants; within which were horrible and violent winds with their own prince and parents. Again a fiery and corruptible region with its own leaders and nations. In like manner within, a nation full of darkness and smoke, in which dwelt the monstrous prince of all and leader, having around himself innumerable princes, of all of whom he himself was the mind and origin: and these were the five natures of the pestilential land. If he said that the nature of God is an airy or even ethereal body, truly he would be laughed at by all who are able to behold with some sharpness of an already more serene mind the nature of wisdom and truth, stretched out and spread through no spaces of places, great and magnificent without any bulk, not smaller in part and greater in part, but equal through all things to the highest Father, not having one thing here and another elsewhere, but whole everywhere, present everywhere.

choices.why: Fixed glossary term for Mani's realm of evil.

choices.english: the five natures of the pestilential land
choices.why: Preserves the exact number and the source's 'naturae' as 'natures' per glossary.
rejected: five pestilential natures of the earth

choices.why: Glossary 'natura' is 'nature'; keeps the philosophical force of Augustine's argument.
Literal rendering of the superlative; Augustine contrasts God's equality with spatial inequality.

choices.english: some sharpness of an already more serene mind
choices.why: Literal; 'acies' is the mind's keen sight, and 'serenioris' is comparative, matching Augustine's contrast with the unenlightened.
rejected: the gaze of a clearer mind

pass_b_english: What if, with God and our Lord helping me, I show that what he says is not only uncertain but false? What could be found more wretched than this superstition, which not only fails to provide the knowledge and truth it promises, but says things that are violently opposed to knowledge and truth? This will appear more clearly in what follows. For he says: “Along one side and border of that illustrious and holy land was the land of darkness, deep and immense in size, in which dwelt fiery bodies—pestilential races, that is. Here were infinite darknesses flowing from the same nature, immeasurable, with their own offspring; beyond these were muddy and turbid waters with their inhabitants; within these were horrible and violent winds with their prince and parents. Again, a fiery and corruptible region with its leaders and nations. In the same manner, further inward, a race full of darkness and smoke, in which dwelt the monstrous prince of all and leader, having around him innumerable princes, of all of whom he himself was the mind and origin. These were the five natures of the pestilential land.”

If he said that the nature of God is an airy or even ethereal body, he would certainly be laughed at by all who are able to perceive, with some sharpness of an already more serene mind, that the nature of wisdom and truth is not stretched out or spread through any spaces of place, is great and magnificent without any bulk, is not smaller in one part and larger in another, but is equal to the highest Father in all things, and does not have one thing here and another elsewhere, but is whole everywhere and present everywhere.

problems.why: The Latin has 'princeps omnium et dux' = 'prince of all and leader.' 'Dux' is appositive to 'princeps,' not a separate figure.
problems.fix: the monstrous prince of all and leader

edits.old: the monstrous prince of all and their leader
edits.new: the monstrous prince of all and leader

fixed: Changed 'their leader' to 'leader' because the Latin 'princeps omnium et dux' has 'dux' as an appositive to 'princeps,' not a separate figure.

last_rejected.why: suo is singular reflexive referring to venti; English 'their' is ambiguous, could refer to waters.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Their' naturally refers to nearest antecedent 'winds' in context; Latin suo also ambiguous by position.

last_rejected.why: suis is singular reflexive referring to aquae; English 'their' is ambiguous, could refer to darknesses.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Their' naturally refers to nearest antecedent 'waters'; Latin suis equally ambiguous by position.

last_rejected.why: 'Latus' means side/flank, not border; 'border' suggests boundary line, but Mani describes a spatial region alongside.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Latus' can mean side/border; rendering as 'border' alongside 'side' is within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: Here were infinite darknesses flowing from the same nature
last_rejected.source_quote: hic infinitae tenebrae ex eadem manantes natura
last_rejected.why: 'Hic' means 'here' spatially, not 'from the same nature'; 'manantes' modifies tenebrae, 'natura' is ablative with 'ex eadem natura' = 'from the same nature'.
last_rejected.fix: Here infinite darknesses flowing from the same nature
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly reads 'flowing from the same nature'; 'hic'='here' spatially; no actual error.

last_rejected.quote: within these were horrible and violent winds
last_rejected.source_quote: quarum interius uenti horribiles ac uehementes
last_rejected.why: 'Quarum' refers back to waters, so 'interius' = further within/beyond them, not 'within these' winds; structure is layered regions.
last_rejected.fix: further within these were horrible and violent winds
last_rejected.ruling: 'Within these' for 'interius' conveys layered regions adequately; not a major meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: In the same manner, further inward
last_rejected.why: 'Pari more' = in like manner/similarly, but 'introrsum' = inward, not 'further inward'; also 'gens caliginis' = race of darkness, not 'race full of darkness'.
last_rejected.fix: In like manner inward, a race of darkness
last_rejected.ruling: 'Further inward' for 'introrsum' is acceptable; 'full of darkness' for 'caliginis' is paraphrase within range.

last_rejected.why: 'Circase' = around himself; 'principes' = princes, but the syntax 'circase... principes' = having princes around himself.
last_rejected.ruling: English 'having around him innumerable princes' correctly renders 'habens circase innumerabiles principes'.

last_rejected.quote: These were the five natures of the pestilential land
last_rejected.source_quote: haeque fuerunt naturae quinque terrae pestiferae
last_rejected.why: 'Terrae pestiferae' is genitive with naturae: five natures of the pestilential land; but 'haeque' = 'and these', referring to the five regions just listed.
last_rejected.fix: And these were the five natures of the pestilential land
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly renders genitive 'naturae quinque terrae pestiferae' as 'five natures of the pestilential land'.

last_rejected.quote: with some sharpness of an already more serene mind
last_rejected.why: 'Qualicumque' = with whatever/some; 'acie' = sharpness/edge, but 'iam serenioris mentis' = of a now more serene mind, not 'already more serene'.
last_rejected.fix: with whatever sharpness of a now more serene mind
last_rejected.ruling: 'Already more serene' for 'iam serenioris' is acceptable; 'iam' can mean 'now/already'; not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: equal to the highest Father in all things
last_rejected.why: 'Per omnia' = in all respects/throughout, not 'in all things'; 'aequalem... patri' = equal to the highest Father.
last_rejected.fix: equal to the highest Father in all respects
last_rejected.ruling: 'In all things' for 'per omnia' is within normal range; meaning 'in all respects' is preserved.
